mods.name: Bob's Pipes
mods.description: Bob's Pipes: a reusable carved corewood pipe, made at the workbench. Prepare Meadow, Honeywood or Cloudberry pipe tobacco at Quad's Cigar Rolling Table. Use a tin to pack an empty pipe, then use your hotbar pipe near a burning fire or holding a torch to light it. Use it again to put it out and save the unfinished bowl. The lit pipe rests in your mouth, with a small ember, quiet smoke, occasional exhalations and a slowly seasoned finish. Combat, swimming and exposed rain put it away. Small blend bonuses, configurable down to cosmetic only. Requires Quad's Cigars; with its smoking API (v1 or newer), pipes and cigars share one active smoke.
mods.notes: 0.1.5: Works with Quad's Cigars under its new id (com.quad.cigarsmoking, from 0.3.1), and still with older copies (com.dhack.cigarsmoking).
mods.restart: Adds saved pipe and tobacco item prefabs. Install Bob's Pipes and Quad's Cigars on the host and every player, then restart Valheim before loading the world.

mods.name: BuildShapes
mods.description:
Stave temple designer: equip your hammer, choose F4 → Stave temple, and Shift+click the floor-plan corners in boundary order. L opens the settings. The solver fits a tall central chamber into the outline, with lower surrounding roofs and one or two narrowing tower crowns. Each upper tower has an aperture through the roof below, preserving an open interior. Concave outlines work when they have room for the rectangular chamber; the remaining wings stay inside the drawn footprint and get passages into the chamber.

Choose 4 / 6 / 8 m chamber height, one / two tower crowns, and Open surrounding galleries. Galleries reserve a 2 m covered walk around the chamber, with low outer rails; turning them off encloses the side rooms. Keep the chamber at least 2 m taller than the side wings. One crown needs a 6 m-wide chamber: start with at least 10 × 10 m when galleries are on. Two crowns need a 10 m-wide chamber, core-wood framing and at least 14 × 14 m with galleries. A 14 × 18 m outline is a good first design. Too-small outlines explain which setting to change.

Intricacy, roof pitch, layered eaves, swept gable beams, porch and native dragon/raven carvings use the existing controls. Auto uses unlocked materials, including reinforced timber for tall staves. Columns avoid the doorways and central aisle; native support estimates still block unstable plans. Plan shell creates one normal-cost BuildOrders plan, subject to the existing 2,048-piece budget. Temple outlines/settings use saved Hallwright drafts and live draft sharing. This style is a single open chamber; choose Longhouse for storeys or a basement. ClaudeTools supports `hall options style=temple chamber=6 crowns=1 gallery=on`, and status reports the solved chamber and tower height.

Live draft sharing: other players with BuildShapes 0.5.8+ see your corner posts, outline, roof/storey guides and piece previews as cyan visuals labeled with your name. Sharing is on by default across Hallwright, Curve, Arch, Mirror and Repeat. Hallwright options offer Share my draft and Include piece previews; F7 exposes send/receive and piece-preview toggles under Shared drafts. Layout sends only guides and hidden roofs stay hidden. These visuals have no colliders, terrain effects, costs or build actions; Plan shell/L still creates normal shared BuildOrders ghosts. Drafts clear on submission/exit/unload and expire after disconnects. Viewers draw the nearest four drafts within 120 m, with at most 4,096 shared pieces visible; turn off piece previews for guides alone. Only designers need BuildShapes for submitted BuildOrders plans, but live drafts require it on designer and viewer.

Saved Hallwright drafts: outlines, entrance hints and settings auto-save per character and world. F4 → Resume saved Hallwright draft reopens the local preview after F6/restarting or exiting. Reopening changes no terrain or shared plans; terrain/support/recipes are checked again. Delete clears the outline and saved draft; successful Plan shell removes the saved draft. Shape input pauses during a planner-only reload or another planner menu, preserving markers. Large-shell capability is checked before basement excavation.

Layout guides: terrain-height corner markers have amber posts at least 4 m tall, extending to taller planned walls. Floor and storey outlines show the boundary, with ridge/gable guides following the roof settings. Corner posts remain visible through terrain and buildings. Select Materials, Ghosts or Layout in Hallwright options; Layout hides the piece meshes so the footprint and building volume stay easy to read. Door markers have tall posts too. Guides have no collision or piece cost and can be shared with other BuildShapes players.

Mark entrances: after drawing a Hallwright outline, Ctrl+click near an exterior wall for each desired doorway (up to eight). The solver snaps within 4 m to metre positions and jointly preserves clear openings, interior stairs and external decks. Preview outlines show fitted door positions. Ctrl+click a marker again or Ctrl+Backspace removes it; options also list removals. The first marker gets the covered porch and sets the basement entrance ground height. All marked doors use the selected Door/Gate setting. Each receives stairs or a cellar deck and apron. With no entrance markers, the original entrance-edge selector remains available. ClaudeTools: hall doors <x,z>... or hall doors clear; hall entrances checks native built passage clearance.

Hallwright now supports one to three storeys and an optional 3 m stone basement. Interior native stairs have landings, clear headroom openings and guards; structural columns avoid the walking route. A straight flight needs 2 × 8/10/12 m including landings for 2/3/4 m storeys. Concave floors and roofs stay within the drawn cell union. High intricacy adds daylight windows, carved bands and King’s hall knotwork with unlocked darkwood panels. All native pieces count toward materials, support and the 2,048-piece shell limit.

Basement checkbox: stone slabs and retaining walls below the main floor, interior stairs, entrance deck and a level apron with the ground floor just above the outside entrance terrain. Previewing changes no ground. Plan shell excavates the footprint (plus retaining-wall clearance) and grades the entrance before adding shared ghosts; failed submission restores it. Choose a clear, dry, loaded site within native 8 m digging limits. Requires unlocked stone walls/floors and wooden stairs. Confirmation acquires loaded terrain through the native ownership API and refreshes/rechecks it before excavation; restoration does the same after validating access and saved heights. You can plan while joining another player. Ownership changes mid-operation stop the edit and retain recovery.

U only removes unbuilt ghosts. Restore ground in Hallwright options restores the saved excavation after clearing any built cellar; it refuses overlapping later edits or existing buildings. Recovery survives F6/restarts in one per-world record under BepInEx/config. Keep excavation discards that record and allows another cellar. Reopen Hallwright to find recovery even without drawing another outline. The updated planner PR retains completed add-on records for Takedown. ClaudeTools: hall options storeys=1|2|3 basement=on|off detail=0..4; hall stairs/pieces inspect native built pieces; hall restoreground/keepground are explicit terrain actions.

Draw curves and arches, mirror pieces, repeat decorations, and design a whole Viking timber hall from a floor plan as shared BuildOrders ghosts. Requires BuildOrders with its planning and ghost-selection APIs.

With a hammer and building piece selected, close the piece menu. F4 opens a picker for Hallwright, Stave temple, Curve, Arch, Mirror, and Repeat. Choose a mode; modifiers are no longer needed. F4/Escape closes the picker, and selecting the current mode resumes its preview. Switching modes clears the local preview; submitted ghosts remain. Use Exit shape mode in the picker, or Escape outside options, to return to normal building. Shift+click marks points, L submits, U removes your last shape's unbuilt ghosts, and Backspace removes the last marker. Exit shape mode to build normally with E.

Hallwright: choose it in F4 with the hammer equipped, then Shift+click square corners in boundary order. The first edge sets the rotated 2-metre grid; subsequent edges snap to its two directions. Concave L/U outlines work. L opens the settings, or click the first corner again to finish drawing. Backspace removes a corner; Delete clears the outline. From four corners onward, an invalid outline automatically shows its reason at the centre of the screen while drawing; L is not needed to see it. Adjust walls (2–4 m), roof pitch (26°/45°), Gabled/Tiered silhouette, entrance type and edge, foundation lift and an intricacy dial (Simple, Crafted, Ornate, Grand, King’s hall). Exact foundation lift and fine nudges use the same numeric controls as Arch/Repeat. The shell previews using the real meshes, with materials/ghost and roof visibility buttons. Auto entrances use an unlocked 3 m gate when wall height is 3 m or taller; choose Door or Gate explicitly. Gates require at least 3 m walls. The opening and header fit the actual native piece height. Tiered roofs raise the central roof by 1 m above low side aisles on wings at least 6 m wide; matching gables, vertical roof-step walls, shaped rafters and structural inner colonnades support the raised tier. Narrow wings stay gabled. Its floors, exterior walls and entrance, joined rectangular roof wings, gable infill, trusses, terrain-reaching foundations and entrance steps are fitted together. Small odd-width gable peaks are intentionally vented. Intricacy adds knee braces, radiating gable timberwork, darkwood arches and raven crests when unlocked.

Longhouse details: toggle Deep roof overhangs, Covered entrance porch, and Sweeping gable timberwork independently. Overhangs extend 2 m with native 26° eave aprons (a 1 m drop) and bracket/outrigger beams; extensions that overlap another wing or the porch are skipped. Walls at least 3 m high preserve 2 m under the side apron. The 4 × 2 m porch needs a straight entrance edge at least 4 m long and clear space outside, adds 8 m² of deck, uses normal floor/roof pieces and braces, and brings its foundations to the terrain. The floor height also samples the porch; entrance steps start at the porch's outer edge. Swept exposed gables at least 4 m wide use curved paths of native 1 m beams with overlapping joints. Ridge ends offer Auto/None/Dragon/Raven: Auto adds an unlocked native carving at Ornate and above, explicit Dragon/Raven require their recipe unlocked, and carvings face outward where they clear other wings. All added pieces contribute their normal material costs and support checks; unresolved collapses still block planning.

Materials default to Auto, based on your character's known hammer recipes. Stronger core-wood posts, stone plinths, darkwood details and reinforced ridge supports are used only when unlocked. Select Timber/Core wood/Stone base/Darkwood to restrict the style. A live normal-cost materials bill and station list accompany the preview. Unlock changes refresh automatically. Foundations raise the floor above the highest sampled ground; terrain stays intact unless Basement is selected; existing pieces are never removed. Native collider contacts, actual material support losses and nearby built supports estimate whether the complete shell stands; extra interior ridge columns are added when necessary, and unresolved collapsing pieces block acceptance. Confirm rechecks the current terrain, support and unlocks, then creates one shared ghost plan and returns to normal building. This estimate is not a substitute for the game's final placement checks.

Hallwright supports 24 corners, 256 floor tiles (1,024 m²), corners up to 64 m along either grid axis from the first corner, 12 roof wings and 2,048 pieces including foundations, within 70 m of the designer. Long ridges span the complete outline instead of splitting at 24 m; roof width still follows unlocked structural materials. The piece budget remains separate: large or tall ornate halls may need lower intricacy. Move toward the centre before confirming a large outline. Diagonal/self-crossing outlines, unloaded or protected ground, excessive foundations and stretched beams are rejected. Large shells need BuildOrders' TryCreateBuildingShell API (provided in the Hallwright planner PR); older planners can accept shells up to their 256-piece cap. U removes the last plan's unbuilt ghosts; select Hallwright again after confirming to use U. Local preview state clears on F6, death, world changes or switching modes; an unsubmitted Hallwright draft can be reopened from its saved copy. ClaudeTools exposes hall catalog/rectangle/outline/options/status/resume/ui/clear/confirm/undo and a hallpreview camera frame for testing.

Curve: select a beam/pole and mark start, bend, end. Native-length beams follow the curve in 3D with overlapping joints. Requires two endpoint snap points and a span of 0.25–8 metres.

Arch: select a beam/pole and Shift+click start and end. The height panel opens automatically. Center rise (0–32 m) is measured above the line between the endpoints; a gold guide marks the midpoint. Adjust the slider, type an exact height then Enter/Apply, or use ±0.05 m buttons (Shift: 0.01 m). The preview updates live, keeping both endpoints fixed. Confirm applies pending edits and creates shared ghosts. Edit end keeps your chosen rise; Escape closes the panel, L reopens it, and Cancel exits; F4 opens the mode picker. This is a vertical parabolic curve; unequal endpoint heights are supported. Beams keep their native lengths with overlapping joints, so the center line approximates the curve. Ends must be horizontally separated, and tight bends or too-long beams are rejected.

Mirror: mark two points for a vertical mirror plane, then Ctrl+click built pieces or visible ghosts to toggle source selection. Thin wire boxes show sources; heavier boxes preview copies. Ctrl+Backspace removes the last selection. Reflection axes and pivot compensation follow native snap layouts, fixing triangular under-roof walls and sloped beams while preserving ordinary roof pitch; mesh bounds are a fallback. Asymmetric carvings and handed meshes keep their original geometry, so inspect the ghosts before building.

Repeat: mark start, bend, end with any normal building piece selected. An options panel opens automatically beside the preview: choose a Path anchor (piece origin, visual center, or a native snap point), spacing, yaw, pitch, roll, and whether to turn with the curve. Changes preview live. For precise adjustments, type a value then Enter/Apply, or use ± buttons (0.05 m / 1°; Shift: 0.01 m / 0.1°). Sliders keep exact values until dragged. Confirm applies pending numeric entries and submits, Edit path replaces the end, and Cancel exits. F4 opens the mode picker. Escape closes options without losing the path; L reopens. Slider clicks never mark the world or attack. Spacing fits evenly to both endpoints; the chosen anchor stays on the path after rotation, marked by gold crosses. Choose Bottom for a post base or an end snap for a beam. There is no automatic terrain alignment. Curve-following preserves the seed's initial heading/tilt, then applies rotation offsets. Outside the panel, Ctrl+click copies a built piece/ghost and its orientation; [ / ], Page Up/Down, and Home remain available.

Preview strokes/boxes are approximate and can be shared live; L creates full shared planner ghosts. Curves are limited to 128 metres and Curve/Arch/Mirror/Repeat to 256 pieces; Hallwright has the larger bounds above. Markers/sources require 40-metre reach; the planner checks all output positions, recipes, wards, and no-build areas. Scaled and terrain-operation pieces are excluded. Selections are pose snapshots.

Optional confirmed basements change terrain; built pieces stay intact and normal materials/support still apply. Undo is one submitted shape across all tools and clears on death, world change, or F6. Only the designer needs BuildShapes; participating players should use updated BuildOrders and the selected pieces. Ghost selection, mirror mesh alignment, multiplayer, and fresh-launch behavior need gameplay testing.
mods.notes: 0.6.5: Works with BuildOrders under its new id (com.quad.buildorders, from 1.12.1) and Claude Tools under its (com.quad.claudetools), and still with older copies.

mods.name: ChestSearch
mods.description:
Search nearby chests from one window. Ctrl+F opens your inventory and a search bar with normal item-slot visuals. Type part of an item name to filter separate stacks, then drag a stack onto an empty inventory slot or a matching stack. Hover to see its source chest; use the page buttons for more results.

Default range is 20 metres, adjustable from 5 to 40 in F7. Searches loaded accessible storage containers, including chest inventories and carts; skips wards/private chests you cannot use, busy containers, creature bags, tombstones and recyclers. Up to 64 nearby containers and 512 matching stacks, with 24 slots per page. All typed words must appear in the item's localized name.

Only real chest items are moved. A drag is a visual preview until it lands on your inventory; cancelling, closing, or dropping elsewhere does nothing. Normal chest-owner permission is requested before reloading the source and checking that the selected stack is unchanged. Different occupied slots are rejected; compatible partially full stacks take only what fits. Moving out of range, stale results, denied access and timeouts cancel the transfer.

Native Linux and Windows, no other mod dependency and no custom chest save data. Install on the player using the window; native chest RPCs work with an ordinary host. Ctrl+F and Escape close the search. Mouse drag and keyboard search are supported; controller/touch search are not yet implemented. F6 removes the window and preview without moving items. Compiled and checked against local native assemblies; layout, drag behavior, live ownership transfer, other UI mods and multiplayer still need in-game playtests.
mods.notes: 0.1.0: Ctrl+F chest-search window with localized name filtering, native slot icons/tooltips, source chest labels and paging. Drag real nearby chest stacks into the player inventory through normal chest-owner permission; recheck access, range, stack identity and destination capacity. Preview cancellation, stale-result rejection, bounded scans and F6 cleanup. Native Linux/Windows; configurable 20-metre default range.

mods.name: DualWield
mods.description:
Fight with a weapon in each hand. Pairs of one-handed axes, knives, maces and swords are supported. Two knives fight like the game's Skoll and Hati; two axes, two maces or two swords swing like the Berserkir axes.

Equip a one-handed axe, knife, mace or sword, then equip a second one of the same kind: it goes into your off hand, replacing your shield or torch. You need 20 in that weapon skill (Clubs for maces); for axes, half of your Woodcutting counts too (Axes + half of Woodcutting must reach 20). Below it you are told how your total is made up. Hold Left Alt while equipping to replace your main weapon instead. Putting away the main weapon moves the off-hand one across. Equipping a shield, torch or another kind of weapon ends dual wielding as usual.

Balance: each hit is worth 62% of both weapons' damage combined, about 1.24× one weapon when they are equal, normalized against the dual move set's own combo. Every swing costs 1.3× the main weapon's stamina. Both weapons wear down. Blocking uses only the main weapon's weak block, shown with both weapons raised, so a shield is still the defensive choice. The skill you train is the pair's own. Mixed pairs are not supported yet.

Install for every player: the off-hand weapon and the dual stance are seen by others through the game's own equipment and animation sync, and the off-hand position needs this mod to look right. The damage share, stamina, skill requirement, swap key, and each kind's off-hand position and rotation can be changed in F7. Compiled and checked against the local game; the off-hand look, move sets, balance and GearSlots interaction still need in-game playtests.
mods.notes: 0.1.2: Maces and swords pair up too. Two one-handed maces (Clubs 20) or two one-handed swords (Swords 20) go into both hands and swing with the Berserkir axes' moves, with the same damage, stamina, wear and weak block as axes. Each kind has its own off-hand position and rotation in F7.

mods.name: Farmhand
mods.description:
Lay out a whole crop plot with your cultivator: select a crop, then Shift+click corners in boundary order. Concave outlines work. Shift+J plants the previewed layout as you walk through the field, within normal cultivator reach. The first edge sets row direction; spacing leaves a half-cell border and increases for larger growth radii. Green dots are within reach; amber dots wait until you approach; blocked spots turn red.

Escape pauses, and Shift+J resumes without repeating successful spots. Recover stamina automatically; add seeds or repair the tool when paused. Backspace removes the last corner; Delete clears the plot. At most 32 corners, 512 spots and 400 square metres by default. Self-crossing outlines are rejected. Plot previews and progress clear on reload or changing characters.

Without a marked plot, Shift+J still plants a short row. Shift+U harvests and replants nearby mature crops; add Left Ctrl to harvest only. Unhealthy crops get helpful labels.

Every successful planting uses ordinary seeds/materials, stamina and cultivator durability. Cultivation, biome, sunlight, space, obstacles and wards still apply. Harvest drops remain world items. BuildFromChests can supply seeds. Select a crop or seed crop, not a tree or vine; turn off BuildOrders plan mode. No extra mod is required on the host or peers.
mods.notes: 0.2.2: Keeps its place before and after BuildOrders under BuildOrders' new id (com.quad.buildorders, from 1.12.1), and still with older copies.

mods.name: Gary
mods.description:
Gary the Greydwarf is a purple forest companion: friendly, defensive, impossible to kill, and occasionally generous with snacks. Uses the game's native Greydwarf body, movement, weapons, and animation; no API key or external service required.

F3 summons one Gary per player, or recalls that same Gary beside you. Shift+F3 tells him to stay where he is; F3 resumes following. Both keys are configurable. Calls need clear dry ground nearby. He waits outside dungeons and for you to respawn; use F3 to call him after a portal trip.

You, other players, and Quad’s AICompanion characters can walk through Gary, so he cannot block doorways or push you around. Terrain/enemy collisions and petting stay active.

Gary follows quietly until a hostile creature actually damages his player or Gary himself. He defends against that attacker for up to 30 seconds and stays within a bounded defense radius. He can defend himself while waiting, including outside a dungeon or while his player is dead/offline, and resumes waiting afterward. He does not pick fights with nearby wildlife, players, or tamed friends. Friendly player/pet hits do not hurt him.

At 20% health, Gary abandons combat and tries to flee 40 metres from you. Damage cannot take his health below 5%, and native death checks are suppressed for Gary alone. He heals rapidly at a safe distance, slowly while escaping, and comes back at 90%. If his zone unloads, a saved three-minute recovery deadline lets him heal before being recalled. Calling him does not interrupt his retreat.

Gary gathers real raspberries, blueberries, mushrooms, and loose feathers into a saved six-item stash, then occasionally tosses one near your feet (roughly every 3–5 minutes). At most two pockets hold feathers; when food is available, feathers are a 20 percent gift choice. Empty pockets produce no gifts. Loose feathers must already be owned by his simulator and within two metres as he passes; player-dropped items, nearby players, bases, placed/custom items and Gary's own gifts are skipped. He skips nearby players/protected plants, never claims plant ownership, and preserves normal regrowth and resource scaling. Gifts land as normal ground items; both stash and cooldown survive F6/world saves.

Look at Gary and press your normal Use key (E) to pet him: a friendly pat, quiet forest chirp, purple sparkles, and a brief happy dance with no stat bonus. He greets you after absences/dungeons, celebrates foes he fought and your nearby victories over huge enemies, and occasionally chirps/looks toward nearby visible danger. Huge enemies make him nervous; warnings never start attacks.

When you settle near a burning fire or hearth, Gary finds clear ground beside it and relaxes. When you pause to build, he watches from the side, away from your placement ghost; walking away resumes following. His retreats choose reachable dry ground away from both you and danger, preferring cover. Combat and healing interrupt social activities. Campfire, building, reactions, and warnings have separate settings.

Within 90 metres, Gary can notice a loaded burial chamber, sunken crypt, troll cave, or frost cave entrance. He leads a little way ahead, waits if you lag behind, and gives up if the route is obstructed. Confirmed fully looted dungeons are skipped; unfinished dungeons can be revisited after a ten-minute shown-entrance cooldown. Counts unopened chest contents, loose treasure, cores, scrap piles, collectible cave materials, and removable valuables; ignores enemies, regrowing food, and ordinary furniture salvage. Reads saved chest item counts without opening/generating loot. Incomplete/unloaded scans stay unknown and eligible. Up to 512 cleared entrances are saved per player/world with your character; older visits need a complete scan. No distant locations/map pins; he waits outside.

Install Gary on the host/dedicated server and participating clients for multiplayer. The server authenticates commands and finds the existing saved Gary, including unloaded zones, before spawning. Creature simulation and gifts run only on its network owner. Uses tagged vanilla Greydwarf saves, so removing the mod leaves a normal tamed greydwarf instead of an unknown-prefab object. Special behavior and purple appearance require the mod.

Gary can ride your boat. While following within 12 metres and five metres of vertical reach, he hops to a clear deck spot beside you and stays there through sailing, turns and waves. F3 can call/recall him onto a free deck spot too. He does not take a player seat, control the boat, push its hull, or fight/forage while riding. After a brief grace period he hops onto nearby dry ground or a dock when you disembark. If you fall into the water, die, leave the area or tell him to wait, he stays aboard until you return or recall him. Injured passengers rest/heal aboard rather than fleeing into the ocean. Boarding state survives F6 and world saves; a missing/destroyed ship releases him alive. No transform parenting to the boat. Toggle Companion/RideBoats in F7.

Your Gary has a purple moving marker on the minimap and full map. If he unloads but his saved object is still known, it shows Gary (last seen) at that position; it disappears when no position is known. Only your Gary is shown. The marker is transient, does not become a saved/shared map pin, and cleans up on F6/world/player changes. Toggle Companion/MapMarker in F7.

Gary now has eight more playful habits. F8 throws one actual Wood from your inventory toward reachable ground about nine metres ahead; he chases it, carries the same normal item back and waits for a pat. Fetch is bounded to 16 metres/35 seconds, takes priority over crypt guiding and other idle activities, chases the ground landing while Wood is airborne, retries temporary navigation failures for up to five seconds, requires compatible ownership, and stops for combat, recovery, waiting, boats, portals, or F6; the real Wood stays in the world. There is no item escrow or conjured refund. A returned item can be picked up normally.

Nearby wave, cheer, dance, sit and relax emotes get an awkward Gary imitation. Shift+E on your own built wood pile marks a reachable leaf/branch nest beside it; repeat on that pile to forget it. When you pause nearby for eight seconds, he curls up there. His home reference survives saves/F6; the original pile retains normal materials, support and removal behavior. In rain he looks for a reachable nearby roof while you settle down and shakes dry afterward.

On boats he prefers a clear forward deck spot, watches ahead, chirps at visible seabirds and crouches when waves tilt or lift the hull strongly. He wears a small matte twig-and-feather crown, tiny pouch and ear feather in muted forest colors, using native game materials with emission disabled. He also greets your nearby Quad AICompanion characters, watches their building/gathering work and occasionally imitates their motions. Before a forest gift he briefly holds up a mesh-only preview, then tosses the actual stash item. These activities give no buffs or extra resources; combat/recovery take priority.

Personality activities and Appearance accessories have separate F7 toggles. Fetch key is configurable under Controls; nest marking uses Left Shift plus the normal Use key. Gary's native rig has no wave/sleep/crouch animations, so these use local cosmetic bone poses replicated from bounded activity state. New poses, accessories, nested roofs, boat geometry, F6 and ownership changes need in-game playtests.

Settings are in F7 → Mod settings, or BepInEx/config/com.bobisme.gary.cfg. Compiled and checked against native Linux assemblies, including food-conservation, injury, defense, petting, reaction and retreat policy tests. Appearance, pathfinding, audio, live multiplayer, and save/restart behavior need in-game playtests.

Reforestation: while you are near your bed, Gary now and then plants a real sapling on open wild ground nearby, beside a stump you left when he can, never in your base, near buildings, on farmland or paths. Seeds and cones he picks up let him plant more. Radius, interval and limit are in F7.

Caretaker: around home he stacks deadfall by his nest, gathers freshly dropped harvest for you, replants crops you harvest by hand (with your seeds) and stamps out stray fire. He listens to old trees, shows you berries he found, shouts Timber!, senses Omens' signs and skies, and has opinions about your trophies. Each job is in F7.
mods.notes: 0.5.2: Fixed an error when Gary tidied up deadfall that never regrows (a branch or stone the game removes once picked): he no longer touches it after picking it up.

mods.name: Meadow Golf
mods.description:
Meadow Golf: build a little Viking golf course out of the landscape and your own structures. Craft a carved wooden golf club at a workbench (6 wood, 2 leather scraps). Hammer → Furniture supplies golf tees (2 wood) and cups with linen flags (4 wood, 1 stone).

Shift+E labels a tee or cup as Course:Hole:Par, for example Meadow:1:3. Give both ends the same course name and hole number; the tee sets par. The builder can edit labels. Courses have up to 18 holes, par 2–8; use a unique number for each cup. A matching cup must be within 240 m when you start; the host can find its saved marker even outside your loaded area.

Equip the club and E at a tee to set your colored wooden ball. Stand within 3 m of the stationary ball, aim with the camera, use the wheel to choose Drive / Chip / Putt, then hold left mouse to charge and release to swing. Gentle putts begin at low power; charging takes 1.4 seconds. An amber path and stopping-point ring predict flight, bounces and rolling with the actual ball physics. The HUD distinguishes predicted range (with its sampled power) from distance to the cup. Right click cancels charging. The native swing contact event launches the ball, with a wooden impact and quieter bounce sounds. Prediction is spread across frames; unreliable results show a short direction line. Balls roll, bounce and hit real terrain and buildings; they do not damage anything. Players and creatures pass through balls, and golfers cannot hit someone else's ball. A slow ball entering its linked cup finishes the hole.

G opens the match and scorecard window using Valheim's own wooden inventory panel, recessed score area and fonts. Stand within 5 m of hole 1: [1] starts a 9-hole match, [2] starts 18 holes, and [J] joins the open match. The host checks all saved numbered tees and cups, even outside loaded areas, and names missing/duplicate endpoints or holes longer than 240 m. Each course name identifies one course: use distinct names for separate courses. A front nine may also be played on an 18-hole course. Everyone has a separate painted ball and saved card; a shared match ID groups the results. E at each next tee continues after you finish the current hole. Match play prevents skipping unfinished holes or replaying completed holes. Finishing hole 9 or 18 completes your round. [X] stops your own round and preserves its finished scores; [M] ends the shared match, allowed for its starter, the first tee's builder or the local server host. Ending hides/freezes the balls and keeps the results. [R] refreshes the host scoreboard, including participants whose balls are outside loaded areas; up to eight rows are displayed. G/Escape closes the window. New rounds replace your previous card; stopped participants cannot restart within the same match. End that match and start another for a fresh round.

The landscape matters: uncleared grass has more rolling resistance than cleared ground or built floors; Black Forest/Mistlands rough is heavier, swamp mud is heaviest, and mountain/Deep North snow slows rolls too. Clear a fairway with a hoe, build banked paths or bridges, and use real trees, rocks, walls, ramps and ceilings as obstacles. Gravity and actual colliders drive rebounds and downhill rolls. Entering native water or liquid hazards automatically returns the ball to the last shot's lie for exactly one extra stroke. A flooded tee is rejected. The preview uses the same surface rules and marks a predicted water entry in blue with a +1 warning. Preview liquid levels exclude momentary waves for stable course rules. There are no terrain changes, weather forces or damage to trees/buildings.

For casual practice, E at any tee starts a hole and Ctrl+E starts a fresh practice card, leaving your current match card. Practice replays replace that hole's result; changing courses starts a new card. E on your ball returns it to the last shot's lie for one penalty; E on the same unfinished hole's tee returns it to the tee for one penalty. There is a 99-stroke ceiling. Cup rings are visual and never excavate terrain. Indoor and basement courses use actual floors, rather than lifting the ball to outdoor terrain height.

Install Meadow Golf on the host and every player, then restart before loading a world: the club, tees, cups and balls are new saved prefabs. Mouse/keyboard controls; G is adjustable in F7. No dependency on BuildOrders or Gary. Reloads cancel a charged swing and reattach Golf's scripts to saved pieces/balls. No periodic whole-scene scans; the host indexes saved golf balls once per world/reload in batches.

Compiled on native Linux with rule tests and exact installed-game API checks. See VALIDATION.md for the current Creative test results and remaining remote multiplayer qualification. Optional ClaudeTools commands include golf status, golf match 9|18|join|end|stop|scores, and golf shot drive|chip|putt <power> <dx> <dz>. Disposable roundtest and fixture commands are limited to locally hosted Creative; they do not terraform or modify existing buildings.
mods.notes: 0.2.3: Its Claude Tools commands work with Claude Tools under its new id (com.quad.claudetools, from 1.2.2), and still with older copies.
mods.restart: Adds saved golf club, tee, cup and ball prefabs. Install Meadow Golf on the host and every player, then restart Valheim before loading the world. F6 alone is not the first-install workflow for a shared world.

mods.name: Omens
mods.description:
Signs appear in the world that foretell good or bad things, and what they foretell really happens. Twenty-one omens, from raids you can avert to treasure, a great stag to hunt, a night of northern lights, and a cursed hoard you can choose to take. How you answer them sets the gods' favour, which shapes what comes next.

Every 1.5 in-game days or so, the host places an omen 45 to 85 metres from a player, away from buildings. Walk near it to read it: a message appears on screen for players nearby, a chat line for everyone, and a pin on your map. An omen nobody finds fades after a day without effect.

Bad omens:
Dead troll (Black Forest): trolls raid the nearest base that night, unless you burn the carcass with 5 resin.
Scattered cairn (Meadows, Black Forest, Swamp): skeletons raid, unless you lay the bones to rest with 5 bone fragments.
Abandoned camp (Meadows, Black Forest): greydwarfs raid.
Drained deer (Meadows, Black Forest): at night a hunting pack suited to the base's land comes for it, once someone is home.
Blood-soaked circle (most land): that night the sky turns red, and night creatures spawn twice as often, more at once and stronger. 4 raw meat softens it.
Gnawed carcass (Mountains): wolves raid, unless you leave 3 raw meat for the pack.
Fuling war banner (Plains): Fulings raid, unless you tear the banner down, which brings its three guards at once.
Drowned man (shores): draugr come ashore for the nearest base at night, unless you pay his passage with 10 coins.
Cursed hoard (most land): leave it and nothing happens. Take its coins and gems, and that night a ghost leads the dead to whoever took it.
Unlit grave candles (Black Forest, Swamp, Mountains): ghosts haunt the base, unless you relight them with 3 resin.
Scorched circle (Black Forest, Swamp, Plains): surtlings raid.
Lightning-split oak (most land): that night Thor's storm breaks, with lightning striking near anyone in the open. 20 coins buried at the oak stop the strikes.
Ship with black sails (shores): its draugr crew comes ashore for the nearest base at night, unless you light a warning beacon with 20 wood.

Good omens:
Circling ravens (open sky): players nearby are rested, and 250 metres of land is revealed on their maps.
Gulls over the shore: real fish are stranded on the shore.
Dancing lights: a light drifts off to a real treasure chest of that land nearby, pinned on the map.
Shed antler (Meadows, Black Forest): a great two-star stag appears nearby, dropping a hard antler and its trophy.
Fallen star: ore suited to the land lies cooling in the ash.
Cloaked wanderer: he vanishes as you approach; everyone nearby learns every skill 50% faster for 20 minutes.
Forgotten shrine: leave 3 honey for the gods: everyone nearby is rested, and the gods' favour rises.
Humming rune stone: that night the northern lights fill the sky: half the night creatures, faster healing and learning.

Omens that return: a bad omen left to come to pass can come back worse near the home it struck, likelier the less the gods like you.

The rune bones (workbench: 6 bone fragments, 2 resin): cast them to learn which way the nearest omen lies, whether it is good or bad, how the gods see you, and what tonight holds.

The gods' favour: answering omens pleases the gods, and ignoring warnings or robbing the dead angers them. Favoured worlds see fewer bad omens and bigger gifts; forsaken worlds see more omens, with stronger packs.

About 60% of omens are bad, chosen among those that fit the spot. A bad omen comes at nightfall when seen by day, or a few minutes later when seen at night, to the nearest workbench or bed within 1,500 metres of the sign. Raids are the game's own, with their usual messages and music, and never interrupt one already running. A world with raids turned off gets only good omens. Signs are made from the game's own models and cannot be mined, looted or built on.

Install on the host and every player. The host decides everything and keeps a small record per world in BepInEx/config/omens. Frequency, the bad chance, how long signs wait, raid reach and each omen can be changed in F7.
mods.notes: 0.6.2: Its Claude Tools commands work with Claude Tools under its new id (com.quad.claudetools, from 1.2.2), and still with older copies.

mods.name: Local Portals
mods.description:
Local Portals: tall wooden mirrors you can see through and walk through, with no loading screen. Built with the hammer next to the game's portal (workbench nearby; 10 fine wood, 6 greydwarf eyes, 1 surtling core).

Build two within 80 m of each other and the second links to the first; one glows blue, the other orange. Or name them like the game's portals (look at one and press E): two mirrors with the same name are linked, and a name links just two, so a base can have as many pairs as it likes. The mirror tells you what it is linked to, or why it is not.

The glass shows the other side as it really is from where you stand, live, from any angle and distance, with the world's light and fog. Walk into it and you step out of the other mirror, moving and looking the same way, carrying your speed (and your fall). The camera follows you through: for a moment it looks through the first mirror at you coming out of the second, and if the second mirror is in its way from behind, it is cut away. While you are partway through, the part of you that has gone in is seen coming out of the other mirror, on every player's screen, and nothing of you shows behind either one.

The mirrors are solid from behind and at the sides; only their glass lets you through, from the front. Only players go through, not items, creatures or carts (you cannot go through pulling a cart). Both ends must be loaded, which 80 m keeps true.

Each live view draws the world again: about 0.7 ms a view at 4K in testing. Settings: how many mirrors show a live view at once (2), their sharpness, and the body doubles.

Everyone in a multiplayer game needs the mod: a host without it deletes the mirrors when their area loads. Removing the mod removes built mirrors.
mods.notes: 0.1.2: A mirror can stand right against a wall: walls just behind its glass no longer stop you before you are through (you had to get your middle past the glass, and the wall held you back). Floors and the ground still hold you up.

mods.name: Passenger Cart
mods.description:
A passenger cart, built with the hammer next to the regular cart (workbench nearby; 30 wood, 16 bronze nails, 4 deer hide).

It is the game's cart made 30% bigger in every direction, with two plank benches inside: seats for four passengers, facing the handle. One player pulls it like the regular cart while the others ride. Look into the cart at a seat and press E to sit; move or jump to get off, and you step down beside the cart on your own side. A seat someone is sitting in shows as taken.

It has twice the regular cart's health, and it is steadier: a wider track, bigger wheels, a lower centre of mass and damped rocking, so it rolls back upright from knocks that would tip the small cart. Passengers' bodies never push the cart around, on any player's screen. If it does go over, passengers are thrown off.

The cart's storage is opened from the cargo crates behind the back bench (same size as the regular cart's). The load pile the regular cart shows as it fills is left out, since the seats are where it would be.

Everyone in a multiplayer game needs the mod: a host without it deletes passenger carts when their area loads. Removing the mod removes built passenger carts.
mods.notes: 0.1.2: Its Claude Tools commands work with Claude Tools under its new id (com.quad.claudetools, from 1.2.2), and still with older copies.

mods.name: PolygonLeveler
mods.description:
Mark a convex polygon with your hoe, level it horizontally, or flatten it into a smooth sloped plane.

Hold a hoe. Left Shift + left click places a marker. L levels it to the first marker's height. Shift + L fits the closest plane to the current ground, removing bumps while keeping the average slope; the outline updates to that plane. U undoes the last polygon. Backspace removes the last marker and Delete clears the outline. All keys are configurable.

Uses normal terrain saving and network ownership, checks wards and the game's height limits, preserves ground paint, and edits only terrain-grid vertices inside the convex boundary. The visible edge follows the terrain's triangles. Costs one hoe use per polygon, with no stone cost.

Undo restores original heights and smoothing without refunding the hoe use. It refuses conflicting edits and checks current ward permissions and distance. Undo history lasts ten minutes, clears on reload, and requires the original terrain owner to remain available. An interrupted undo can be retried. Only leveling done with this version can be undone.

The fitted plane minimizes squared vertical height changes over the selected ground vertices, counting tile seams once. Polygons too narrow to define a plane are rejected. Install 0.1.3 or newer on the host and participating players for Shift + L in multiplayer. Markers are local previews and disappear on reload. Changes to the ground persist normally. Gameplay and multiplayer still need an in-game playtest.
mods.notes: 0.1.3: Shift + L flattens the current ground to a least-squares fitted plane, preserving its average slope. L still levels horizontally to the first marker. Tile seams count once in the fit, the outline shows the fitted plane, normal terrain limits are checked for every target height, and U undoes either action. Multiplayer owners need 0.1.3 for fitted planes.

mods.name: Shieldwall
mods.description:
A game within the game: build a Warstone, raise towers with war staves around it, and hold the line when a horde comes for it.

The Warstone (hammer, misc; 30 stone, 10 wood, 5 flint, 5 resin, near a workbench) is a standing stone that wards your home. Everyone within 40 metres gets faster health and stamina regeneration, and with each siege the stone holds (its marks), carry weight, eitr regeneration and armor. Set it under a roof with a fire burning within 10 metres and the ward is twice as strong and adds comfort. One Warstone to a home.

Raise the stone's level (1 to 5) by building its upgrades within 10 metres: a war banner, a trophy totem, a horned brazier and a rune obelisk, each paid in warshards. The level decides how many war staves the stone can feed (2 to 10), how far (26 to 50 metres), which staves it can craft and how strong they can be made.

War staves are huge relics, too heavy to wield. Set them in stave sockets, stone pedestals you build on the ground, on walls or on top of towers, at least 5 metres apart. Use a socket to open its slot and choose the stave (the game's own chest window), Shift+Use to strengthen it in place with warshards. Staves fire on raiders and monsters in reach, aim at whoever is closest to the stone, count their kills, and never hurt players, companions, tames or buildings:
Ember stave (level 1): fireballs that splash.
Frost stave (level 2): a fast stream of ice shards that chill.
Hearth stave (level 2): mends you, your companions, your tames and, in a siege, the stone.
Thunder stave (level 3): heavy bolts at the strongest foe in 42 metres.
Blast stave (level 4): bombs that burst over the crowd.
Any other staff that throws something can be set in a socket too, weakly.

Shift+E on the stone opens the war council, where you sound its war horn. A rift opens 60 to 95 metres away and a horde gathers, the strongest your world has unlocked: greydwarfs at first, then the Black Forest's host, the drowned dead, a mountain pack, a Fuling warband, the swarm of the mist and the Charred legion. After 90 seconds it marches on the stone in four to eight waves, ending with a warchief. Turn on ShowRoad in F7 and a glowing line shows the road it will take and bends as you build: walls turn it aside, and where the road is shut a red line marks where they will break through. They fight what stands close, smash what blocks the way, and strike the stone when they reach it. Sappers go for your towers and tear down what holds them up, a raider a stave keeps hitting may turn on its tower, warchiefs strike buildings half again as hard, bats, drakes, deathsquitos and gjall fly over the walls, and diggers raise ramps over moats and dig at the stone's foot: undermine a Warstone (or dig your moat too close) and it topples, cracks and loses a mark. The game's own boss bar counts the waves and the stone's strength, with the game's raid music; the stone names what the next wave holds, and its horn can call the next wave early for bonus warshards.

Hold until the last of them falls and spoils appear by the stone: a chest of that land with warshards, coins and materials. Each siege held adds a mark: the ward grows and the horde grows. If they break the stone it cracks: its ward weakens until it holds a siege again. Nothing is lost; a fallen tower's stave lies where it stood. The first siege is fought by hand, so it is a proving: a smaller horde from a land or two behind yours. Its warshards teach you the staves.

At the war council the stone offers two boasts to swear before the horn, each a harder siege for more warshards: Blood moon (a star more on every raider), Fog of war (a mist; staves see two thirds as far), Burrowers, Black wings, Chosen chief (no blow touches him while his guard of three lives), No respite and Bare stone. Each siege held earns a boon: choose one of three and the stone keeps it for good, from stronger staves of one kind to more staves fed, farther reach, a tougher stone or a stone that mends with every raider slain. Every siege ends with its saga in the game's own rune-stone window: who slew how many (each player, companion and stave), the mightiest stave, the stone's closest call and what each warshard was for.

Veteran staves: a stave keeps its kills wherever it stands, and at 25 slain becomes a Veteran with a name of its own, at 100 an Elder and at 300 a Legend, each rank striking 10% harder and burning brighter.

Once you have a Warstone, a base raid that would hit near it becomes a siege at the stone instead, with three minutes' warning (needs Shieldwall on the host).

Sieges run on the game of the player nearest the stone, so they work on a dedicated server without the mod (away from the middle of the world); a game hosted by a player needs Shieldwall on the host, and everyone who joins in needs it too. Warnings, wave pacing, the most raiders at once, the time limit and the horn's cooldown are in F7.
mods.notes:
0.4.1: Veteran staves: a stave keeps its kills on itself and at 25 slain becomes a Veteran with a name of its own ("Brand the Hungry"), at 100 an Elder, at 300 a Legend, each rank 10% stronger and brighter. The war council is now made of the game's own crafting panel (its wood, braid, inset boxes, fonts and Craft buttons). The saga closes by itself after half a minute or when you walk off.

0.4.0: The war council: Shift+E on a Warstone at rest opens a small window that names the horde to come and offers two boasts to swear before you sound the horn, each a harder siege for more warshards (Blood moon, Fog of war, Burrowers, Black wings, Chosen chief, No respite, Bare stone). Each siege held earns a boon: choose one of three at the council and the stone keeps it for good (fourteen in all). Every siege ends with its saga in the game's own rune-stone window: who slew how many, the mightiest stave, the closest call and what each warshard was for.

0.3.7: Its Claude Tools commands work with Claude Tools under its new id (com.quad.claudetools, from 1.2.2), and still with older copies.

0.3.6: A new stone's first siege is a proving you can hold by hand: with no marks it meets a horde two lands below the world's own (one below at its first mark, the full horde from its second), in 3 waves of 20 raiders (10 more for each friend). A stone that falls now leaves a warshard for every six raiders slain.

0.3.5: Staves only fire at what they can see: tree crowns, land, rock and buildings anywhere on the line block a shot, and a stave won't lead its shot into a hill. The horde's road line is now a setting, ShowRoad in F7, off by default; the rift's beacon and map pin still show where they come from.

0.3.4: A stave socket can only be built within the Warstone's reach and while the stone has power to spare for it (2 sockets at level 1, 2 more each level); the hammer says why when it refuses. A fed stave glows in its colour with a pulsing light; a sleeping one stands dark as cold iron with no light.

0.3.3: Fixed building the Warstone by hand: it showed no ghost, took its cost and stood nowhere to be seen (it went to about twice your coordinates, 50 m up). The stone's collider is now convex, which the game needs to set a ghost down.

0.3.2: Fixed a Warstone vanishing (and its cost lost) when built in someone else's game. A host's game deletes any object whose prefab it does not know, so a host without Shieldwall deleted the stone as soon as it loaded it. Your game now asks the host whether it has Shieldwall 0.3.2 or newer; if not, the Warstone, sockets and upgrades refuse to be built and nothing is spent. A dedicated server without the mod still hosts sieges, except within 400 m of the middle of the world, where it keeps the land loaded and deletes unknown objects too.
mods.restart: Adds the Warstone, stave sockets, Warstone upgrades, five staves and warshards as saved prefabs. Install on every player who will build or fight at a stone (and on the host for raids to be drawn to it), then restart Valheim before loading the world.

mods.name: Spyglass
mods.description:
A bronze spyglass. Craft it at the forge from 3 bronze. While it is in your inventory, Shift+Z raises it to your eye; Shift+Z or Escape lowers it.

Looking through it narrows the view to 4× optical magnification. The mouse wheel changes it from 2× to 8×, mouse turning slows to match, and a round eyepiece darkens the edges of the screen. The view is from your eyes, so your character never blocks it. You can still walk while looking.

Where you gaze, your map fills in a little: every quarter second, a 30-metre circle around the point you look at is uncovered, up to 600 metres away. The gaze stops at loaded buildings, trees and ground, and beyond them at the world's generated terrain or sea level. Looking at the sky uncovers nothing. Uncovered map is saved with your character like normal exploring. Radius, range, magnification and the eyepiece can be changed in F7.

Shift+Z takes priority over a plain Z from other mods' shortcut helpers, such as GearSlots' quick slot 1, only while Shift is held. The spyglass is closed by opening the inventory, map, menu or chat, by dying, or by losing the item.

Only the player using it needs the mod for looking and crafting. A spyglass dropped on the ground is a world object: the host and nearby players need the mod too, or a host without it deletes it when its area loads. Removing the mod removes spyglasses from saved inventories. Compiled and checked against the local game; the model, icon, view, map reveal and GearSlots interaction still need in-game playtests.
mods.notes: 0.1.2: Fixed the dropped spyglass drawing as flat white shapes: its parts used the bronze bar's shine-particle material instead of the bar's bronze texture. The native item shine is kept. Hot reloads no longer break spyglasses already in the world, and the GearSlots/QualityOfLife key guard patches only each mod's current copy (ScriptEngine renames every reloaded copy), instead of every leftover one.

mods.name: TrophyHall
mods.description:
Hang your trophies and your hall remembers what you have slain.

Creature trophies on item stands you have built inside a base give everyone in that base small themed perks, shown as a Trophy hall status effect that stays with you for 30 minutes after you leave (adjustable), and never shrinks while it lasts. Each kind counts once, however many heads you hang:

Trolls: +30 carry weight. Draugr: slight poison resistance. Wolves: +10% stamina regeneration. Necks and serpents: +10% swim speed. Greydwarfs: +10% woodcutting skill gain. Boars: +10% health regeneration. Deer: +5% movement speed.

At most six perks apply, rarest first. Every kind of trophy also counts toward comfort under a roof: four kinds add +1, eight add +2. Walking into a hall names it after the ward's owner, counts its trophies and lists the creatures fallen there (at most every ten minutes per hall). Boss trophies stay on their altars, where the game uses them for Forsaken powers.

The perks are deliberately small: flavour felt over time, not a change to combat balance. Only the player in the hall needs the mod; it reads the item stands everyone already sees. Range, readings and the whole mod can be changed in F7.
mods.notes: 0.1.3: The perks no longer shrink or vanish as you walk away. Before, the hall was re-read every two seconds from the trophies within 40 m of you, so heading for the door dropped perks one by one, and the whole effect went if the last heads in reach gave none. Now the effect you carry only grows while it lasts (trophies from another hall are added, up to six perks), stays full while you are near any themed trophy in a base, and counts down its 30 minutes once you leave.
